title: The Great Reallocation: Why 2026 Marketing Budgets Are Moving From Demand Gen to Brand
subtitle: Budgets stayed flat for a second straight year. The smartest CMOs moved the money anyway.
excerpt: Marketing budgets barely moved in 2026, but the money that's there is quietly shifting out of demand gen and into brand and positioning. Here's why that reallocation is the correct read on a flat-budget year, and why most Israeli founders are still doing the opposite.

seo.titleTag: The 2026 Budget Freeze: Brand Over Demand Gen | Ran Timor
seo.metaDescription: 2026 marketing budgets are flat. Gartner data shows CMOs shifting spend from demand gen to brand and positioning. Here's why, and what founders should do.
seo.ogTitle: Why CMOs Are Quietly Moving Budget From Demand Gen to Brand
seo.ogDescription: Flat budgets, rising AI expectations, and a reallocation that most Israeli founders haven't noticed yet. The 2026 data on brand versus demand gen spend.

content.intro:
Every CMO I know built their 2026 plan assuming the budget would grow to match the AI ambition their board signed off on. It didn't.

According to Marketing Week's coverage of the Gartner 2026 CMO Spend Survey, marketing budgets rose to just 7.8% of company revenue this year, up from 7.7% in 2025. That's not growth. That's a rounding error dressed up as an increase, for the second year running.

Meanwhile, 56% of CMOs say their organization lacks the budget required to deliver their 2026 strategy. 54% report insufficient resources overall, according to the same Gartner survey. So the ambition went up, the money didn't, and something has to give.

What's giving, if you look closely at where budgets are actually moving, isn't AI spend and it isn't headcount. It's demand gen. And the money is landing in brand and positioning instead.

That reallocation is the most useful signal in B2B marketing right now, and almost nobody I talk to in Tel Aviv has clocked it yet.
content.pullQuote: When the budget freezes, the CMOs who win aren't the ones who cut evenly. They're the ones who cut demand gen and protect positioning.

sections.heading: The Budget Didn't Grow, But Everyone Spent Like It Did
paragraphs: Go back to any 2025 planning conversation and you'll hear the same assumption: AI would make marketing more productive, and productivity gains would justify bigger budgets to scale what worked. Boards bought that story. CMOs built plans around it.

The data says the story was wrong. CMOs are now allocating an average of 15.3% of their budgets to AI initiatives, per Gartner, but only 30% of marketing organizations have the maturity to actually scale those AI investments. The money went into tools and pilots. The infrastructure, the process discipline, and the team capability to turn AI spend into output didn't keep pace.

So you end up with a marketing function that added a new, meaningful line item (AI) without adding new dollars to fund it. Something in the existing budget has to absorb that cost. In most organizations I've seen this year, it's demand gen that's absorbing it, whether the CMO planned it that way or not.

sections.heading: What the Gartner Numbers Actually Say
paragraphs: Strip away the AI narrative for a second and look at the buyer side, because it explains why demand gen is the correct place to cut. According to Sopro's State of Prospecting 2025 report, based on a survey of over 400 senior B2B decision-makers, 65% of buyers say their budgets are tighter than the prior year.

That means the same demand gen spend that used to convert at a given rate is now chasing buyers with less money, less urgency, and more scrutiny on every purchase. Pumping more dollars into paid pipeline generation when your buyers are tightening their own belts is a losing trade. You're not buying more pipeline. You're buying more expensive, slower-converting pipeline.

That's the part of the Gartner data that matters most, and it's also the part that gets buried under the AI headline: in a separate September 2025 Gartner survey of 174 senior marketing leaders, brand awareness came out as the top priority for 2026, specifically framed as a way to strengthen positioning and drive long-term revenue growth in an increasingly AI-mediated buying environment.

Read that framing carefully. CMOs aren't prioritizing brand because it feels good in a flat year. They're prioritizing it because AI search and AI-assisted buying are changing how buyers discover and evaluate vendors, and a company with weak positioning is invisible in that environment no matter how much you spend on ads.

sections.heading: Where the Smart Money Is Moving
paragraphs: Flat budgets force a choice most CMOs have never had to make explicitly: keep funding every existing program at a slightly reduced level, or cut something entirely and protect what actually compounds.

The CMOs I'd bet on are choosing the second option. They're pulling dollars out of paid demand gen, specifically the bottom of the funnel tactics that need constant refueling to keep producing (retargeting, lead-gen ad spend, content syndication, third-party lists), and moving that money into brand and positioning work that doesn't decay the moment you stop spending.

This isn't a rejection of demand gen. It's a recognition that demand gen without clear positioning is just an expensive way to generate confused leads faster. If your message isn't sharp, every dollar you put into acquisition is buying you a bigger pile of prospects who don't understand what you do.

sections.heading: Why Positioning Is the Only Budget-Proof Line Item
paragraphs: Here's the thing about demand gen spend: it's rented, not owned. Stop paying for the ads, the syndication, the SDR outreach tool, and the pipeline stops the same week. It never compounds. It resets to zero the moment the budget line disappears.

Positioning is the opposite. I worked with a cybersecurity company at Series B that had spent 18 months explaining their product as a technical feature: better detection, faster response time, lower false positive rate. Their sales cycles averaged five months and every rep pitched it differently.

We repositioned the company around the business outcome their buyers actually cared about (reduced breach liability, not detection speed), rebuilt the messaging hierarchy, and retrained the sales team on a single narrative. Sales cycles dropped to roughly three months within two quarters. The demand gen spend didn't change. The pipeline volume didn't change much either. What changed was conversion, because the message finally matched how the buyer actually made the decision.

That's the asset that survives a budget freeze. A sharp positioning narrative keeps paying off in every deal, every quarter, with zero incremental spend. It's the only line item in the marketing budget that compounds without needing more headcount or more media dollars behind it.

sections.heading: The Israeli Founder Reflex That's Backwards
paragraphs: I see the same pattern almost every time an Israeli B2B startup closes a round. The founder's first instinct isn't to fix the message. It's to buy pipeline: hire a growth marketer, turn on paid campaigns, book a demand gen agency, and watch the MQL dashboard fill up.

It feels productive. Leads are a visible, countable output, and countable outputs are reassuring to a board that just wrote a check. But the 2026 data is telling you this instinct is backwards, and it was arguably always backwards, just easier to get away with when budgets were expanding and buyers weren't scrutinizing every purchase.

If 65% of your buyers have tighter budgets than last year, and brand awareness is the top priority for the CMOs who are actually paying attention, buying more pipeline before you fix your positioning means you're accelerating into a wall. You'll generate more leads who take one call, hear an unclear pitch, and disappear. Your CAC goes up, your sales cycle doesn't shorten, and the board starts asking why marketing spend isn't converting.

The fix isn't complicated, but it requires discipline most freshly-funded founders don't have in month one: hold demand gen spend flat or cut it, and put the first real marketing dollars into getting the positioning right. Everything downstream, including the demand gen spend you'll eventually turn back on, gets more efficient once the message is clear.

sections.heading: The Reallocation Playbook
paragraphs: You don't need a bigger budget to make this shift. You need to move existing dollars with intent, and you need to do it without adding headcount, because headcount is exactly what a flat-budget year won't support.
Three moves I'd make in this environment, in order:
bullets: Audit demand gen spend by conversion quality, not volume. Cut the channels producing high lead counts and low win rates first. Those are the ones masking a positioning problem with activity.

Redirect the freed budget into a positioning sprint: a focused 4 to 6 week engagement to nail ICP, messaging hierarchy, and competitive differentiation, before a single new dollar goes back into paid acquisition.
Re-brief sales on the new narrative before you turn demand gen spend back on. A sharper message with the same media budget converts better than a bigger media budget with the same confused message.

content.finalThought: I've watched three different companies make this exact reallocation over the past year, moving money out of demand gen and into positioning without adding a single new hire, and in every case the pipeline that came out the other side was smaller but converted faster. That's the trade a flat budget forces you to make. Most founders resist it because pipeline volume feels like progress. It isn't, if the message underneath it isn't clear. If your 2026 budget isn't growing (and for most of you, it isn't), the highest-leverage thing you can do with the dollars you have is fix the story before you buy more attention for it.
